items.title: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob
items.text:
Abstract

This workshop is designed to help development teams move beyond individual productivity gains to creating repeatable, institutional benefits with agentic coding tools. It emphasizes working effectively and responsibly by balancing human ownership and judgment with AI assistance to improve efficiency without sacrificing accountability. The workshop is structured around key phases of AI-driven engineering: requirements gathering, spec creation, implementation, and verification.
path: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob

items.title: Workshop Flow
items.text:
1. Prerequisites: Clone the repo and run setup
  2. Presentation: Slides structured around key phases of AI-driven engineering: requirements gathering, spec creation, implementation, and verification
  3. Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool: Tour the Bob features you'll use throughout the workshop, from the chat panel and approval gates to modes, subagents, skills, code review, and rollback
  4. Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation: Turn a product request for the Finch Financial app into a decided, phased spec by exploring the codebase with subagents, defining validation criteria, and settling the open design questions yourself
  5. Module 2: Spec Implementation: Start a fresh session with Auto-approve on and have Bob build the spec phase by phase, while you check each phase report against the spec
  6. Module 3: Validation: Review the finished build with the built-in /review and an independent reviewer, then decide at a human gate what to fix and route those changes back through the spec
path: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob

items.title: The Problem
items.text: Agentic coding tools unlock remarkable speed, but without a deliberate approach, that speed comes at the cost of human ownership. As developers offload more decisions to the agent, projects become harder to understand, maintain, and trust. The goal of Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is to reclaim that ownership intelligently: establishing clear points in the workflow where the human retains control, while still allowing the agent maximum autonomy everywhere else. SDD is not about slowing down; it's about maximizing agent autonomy without sacrificing project trust or human ownership.
path: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob

items.title: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation
items.text: Translate a vague product request into a spec the agent can build from. Participants use subagents to explore a brownfield codebase, define testable validation criteria, settle the open decisions themselves, and write a phased spec where every criterion traces to a phase.
path: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob

items.title: Module 2: Spec Implementation
items.text: Execute against the spec with the agent handling code changes autonomously. Participants set the autonomy boundary up front, supervise against the spec, and reset cleanly with git when a run derails.
path: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob

items.title: Module 3: Validation
items.text: Take ownership back. Participants read the diff themselves, run the built-in review and an independent one, separate what needs a human decision from what doesn't, and make the ship/no-ship call.
path: Building Production-Ready Software with IBM Bob

items.title: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool
items.text: A walkthrough of the parts of IBM Bob you will see during the workshop. Nothing to run here. Open Bob alongside this page and find each thing as it comes up. The instructor will tour sections 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 live. Section 3 is explained in Module 1, where you'll watch it happen.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 1. The Chat Panel
items.text:
This is where you work. Five things to locate:

  • Chat history. Your requests, Bob's responses, and every action Bob took: file edits, commands, subagent runs. Actions are expandable, so you can see what was read or changed.
  • The task header. Two numbers at the top right: context in use against the window size (for example 21.3k / 270.0k) and the cost of the task so far. Watch the first one during Module 1's subagent fan-out. It's how you see context isolation working.
  • Mode selector, at the bottom left of the input. Which set of permissions Bob is working with (next section).
  • Permissions dropdown, next to the mode selector. One setting per kind of action Bob can take. Off means Bob asks first. On means it proceeds. In an enterprise deployment some of these can be locked by policy. Details in the next section.
  • Approval cards. When Bob wants to do something that isn't pre-approved, a card appears above the input showing exactly what it will do (the command, the file, the subagent task) with three choices: Approve once, Approve for task, or Reject. "Approve for task" is the middle ground: no more prompts for that kind of action until this task ends. Commands can also be added to a global allow or deny list. This card is the human gate, and the workshop is about deciding where to leave it in place.

Also in the input: type @ to reference a file, a folder, @problems (current diagnostics) or @terminal (recent output). Handing Bob a file this way is how you stop it guessing which one you mean.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 2. Modes and Permissions
items.text:
Both controls sit at the bottom of the input. Together they decide what Bob may do and whether it asks first.

Modes. A mode is a set of permissions, not a personality.

Mode Reads Edits files Runs commands Subagents Ask yes no no explore only Plan yes yes no explore only Agent yes yes yes all

Ask is for understanding a codebase without touching it. Plan can write files but not run anything, which makes it right for producing documents. Agent does everything. Bob can switch modes on its own mid-task, and teams can define custom modes with their own tool restrictions in .bob/custom_modes.yaml.

Permissions. Within whatever the mode allows, the Auto-approve Permissions dropdown decides which actions Bob takes without asking: Read, Edit, Execute, MCP, Skill, Todo, Subtask, Subagent, Mode, plus a master Auto-approve switch. Everything off means a card for every action. Everything on means Bob runs until it's done or stuck. Choices made here apply to the current task only. The settings link at the top of the dropdown opens the global version that applies to every task. In Module 2 you'll turn on Auto-approve and watch the whole build run with no clicks.

In the workshop: Module 1 starts in Ask and moves to Plan at the point where a file gets written. Module 2 runs in Agent with permissions on. Module 3's independent reviewer runs in Ask so that it cannot fix what it finds.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 3. Subagents
items.text:
A subagent is a separate agent with its own empty context. Bob gives it one task, it does the reading, and only a summary comes back to your conversation. Everything it read is discarded with it.

Bob spawns subagents sparingly: when a task is self-contained, would flood your chat with content you don't need to keep, and can't be done in a tool call or two. Exploring a codebase is the textbook case. There are two types: explore (read-only, runs on a lighter model) and general (full tools). You approve each spawn unless subagents are pre-approved in the Permissions dropdown.

When several run at once, each appears as a card in the chat with its own line of stats: done or running, tool calls made, tokens used, cost, elapsed time. Expand a card to see its tool calls. Compare the cards' token counts to the context counter in the task header: that difference is the reading that happened inside the subagents and never entered your conversation.

Subagents vs. subtasks

A subagent runs silently and returns a summary. A subtask is a separate conversation thread with its own breadcrumb that you can follow and continue. Subagents for background reading, subtasks for work you want to watch.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 4. Skills, Rules, and AGENTS.md
items.text:
Three ways a repo teaches Bob how it works. All of them live in the repo, so the whole team gets the same behavior.

  • AGENTS.md at the repo root. Loaded automatically on every conversation. Architecture, conventions, commands, how to behave. The workshop repo has one. Open it and skim before Module 1.
  • .bob/rules/. Extra instruction files loaded alongside AGENTS.md. Per-mode variants (.bob/rules-plan/, .bob/rules-agent/) apply only in that mode. Global rules live in ~/.bob/rules/. The workshop repo doesn't use any. AGENTS.md carries everything.
  • .bob/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. A reusable workflow with a name and a description. Bob activates a skill when your request matches its description, and asks first unless skills are pre-approved in the Permissions dropdown. Supporting files (templates, checklists) sit beside it.

Settings → Skills lists everything loaded with its scope. Built-in skills (scope Built-in, always on) include create-plan, the workflow Plan mode runs on entry, and helpers for creating skills, modes, hooks and MCP servers. The workshop repo's interview skill shows with scope Workspace and a toggle. It's the file at .bob/skills/interview/SKILL.md, and you'll use it in Module 1.

The pattern across all three: structure lives in files, so prompts stay short.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 5. Code Review
items.text:
Type /review or open the Review panel from the sidebar. Pick a comparison branch (your current branch, main, a remote), choose whether to include uncommitted changes, optionally attach a GitHub issue to validate against, and start. It runs auto-approved.

Findings land in the Bob Findings tab in the editor's bottom panel, next to Problems and Terminal, grouped by file with a count per file. Select one to read the explanation and suggested fix. Each has three actions: Go to file, Fix with Bob, and Dismiss, and @problems pulls them into the chat.

The reviewer reads the diff and nothing else. It doesn't know what you decided or why, and it is sometimes wrong. Module 3 is built on treating its findings as things to triage, not instructions to apply.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 6. Rollback
items.text:
Every message of yours that led to file changes carries a rollback icon. Click it, confirm, and Bob undoes every file change and removes every message made after that point. The task continues from there as if the later turns never happened. Rollback belongs to the task it happened in. For anything else, the uncommitted working tree and git restore . are the reset.

Also in Bob

Not covered in the workshop, but worth knowing they exist:

  • Prompt enhance: a button that rewrites your prompt before sending. Leave it alone during the demos.
  • Literate coding: lets you write instructions inline in the editor.
  • Code actions: offer lightbulb fixes.
  • Commit messages and pull requests: Bob can draft both.
  • MCP servers: connect external tools and data.
  • Lifecycle hooks: run shell commands at points in a session to log, inject context, or block actions.
  • Bob Shell: brings the same agent to the terminal, sharing task history with the IDE.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: The Codebase
items.text:
Finch Financial is an internal operations console for a fictional neobank. The app is already running with the following functionality built:

  • Sign in via email and password (all users share the password Password123!)
  • Browse and filter customer accounts by status and name
  • Search and filter transactions across all accounts
  • View an account's detail page with transactions, memos, and audit log
  • RBAC: analysts see active and frozen accounts. Supervisors can also see closed accounts. Only supervisors can add memos.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Your Task
items.text:
The workshop builds the Freeze and Unfreeze product request in product-requests.md:

Product request

Freeze and unfreeze customer accounts when suspicious activity is detected.

An ops analyst notices Northgate Properties just sent a $280,000 wire to Cayman Holdings Ltd, with no prior history of transfers anywhere near that size. They can't freeze the account themselves (that requires a supervisor), so they flag it to their supervisor, who logs in and freezes the account with a reason.

Modules 2 and 3 build and review this feature, so everyone works on the same one. The file also holds a second request, flagging suspicious transactions with a supervisor resolution queue, for running the whole loop again on your own after the workshop.

This module takes a product request to a spec in one session. The input is the product request. From it you build a working knowledge of the codebase and the requirements of the feature, and from those you write the spec: the implementation plan. Two halves: understand the ground your feature lands on, then decide and write.

Human ownership is high here by design. You're the arbiter of the design decisions, so that you understand what you're shipping and the comprehension debt stays low. The agent explores, drafts, and asks. You decide.

Stay in Ask mode while you explore (the agent can read the repo but not change it). Switch to Plan mode when it's time to write (it can edit files but not execute anything).

Everything in a grey code block is pasted to Bob verbatim. The Expect and Notice notes under each prompt describe what a good run looks like, so you can tell when you're on track.

Before you start

  • Bob is open on ~/finch-financial inside WSL (see Prework step 6).
  • Mode selector set to Ask. Permissions dropdown: leave Read on and everything else off for this module. You want to see the approval cards.
  • Open AGENTS.md and skim it. Bob loads it on every conversation. It's where the repo's conventions live, which is why the prompts below can stay short.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Part A: Understand (Ask mode)
items.text: Ask mode can read and spawn read-only subagents. It cannot edit files or run commands.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 1. Map the territory with subagents
items.text:
I'm adding the Freeze and Unfreeze feature from @product-requests.md and I'm new to this codebase. Use three explore subagents in parallel and give me only their summaries:
1. The most similar existing feature, traced from the API call down to the database and its tests. Just the files, in order.
2. Rules the code enforces when an account's status or balance changes. One line each, with the file.
3. Existing parts of the app this feature would touch. As a table.
Don't plan or write code yet.

Expect. Bob reads the product request itself, then asks to spawn three explore subagents. Approve each. Three cards appear and run for a minute or so. Then three summaries land in the chat:

  1. Account memos named as the closest feature, with its files listed in order from the shared types through the web client, the route, the service, the audit helper, the repositories, the schema and the tests. That list is the recipe you'll copy.
  2. Rules as one-liners with file references, usually grouped. Somewhere in it is the fact that matters most: nothing in the codebase changes an account's status or balance today, so you're adding the first transition, not extending one.
  3. A table of areas to touch with a reason for each. Expect a few you wouldn't have guessed: the seed data already has frozen accounts, and their reasons currently live in memos. The activity feed already knows how to render a reason. The audit labels need new entries.

Exact lengths and wording vary from run to run.

You don't need to read every rule

Skim the group headings. The detail is there for when a later step cites it, not for you to absorb now.

Why three subagents. This is where context engineering starts, so it's worth understanding what's happening.

  • The context window is the agent's working memory. It's finite, and it's shared by everything in the conversation.
  • Everything Bob reads stays. A file opened in turn one is still there in turn twenty, competing with the spec you're trying to write for the agent's attention.
  • Exploring a codebase means opening twenty files, most of which you'll never need again.

So the reading happens somewhere else:

Main conversation Explore subagent Starts with your whole session so far an empty context and one question Reads the summaries twenty files Keeps the summaries nothing, discarded when done

That is context engineering: deciding what gets to be in the agent's memory, and keeping the rest out. The three questions are independent, so they run in parallel instead of one after another.

Why these three questions. They're the three kinds of requirement, and each is asked for in the shape the next steps can use directly:

Question Kind of requirement Comes back as 1. Most similar feature the precedent: what to copy a file list, in order 2. Rules enforced the constraints: what must stay true one-liners, each with its file 3. Parts it would touch the integration surface: what must change a table

Notice.

  • The context counter in the task header. Add up the tokens on the three cards. Compare to what the main conversation is using. The difference is reading that never entered your context.
  • How Bob characterizes the sibling, something like "supervisor-only write, audited." That phrase is the architecture lesson. Freeze is the same shape with a status change added.
  • Any line reporting an absence. Absences tell you what you're adding from scratch.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 2. Define validation criteria
items.text:
What does this repo already give me to verify a change against? Then turn the expected outcomes in the product request into validation criteria, one per outcome, each with a pass condition.

Expect. Two parts.

  1. What exists: the test commands, the fixtures, and the nearest test file to copy, plus anything about the test setup that would trip you up. Shape varies.
  2. Criteria: one row per outcome in the request, each with a pass condition you could hand to a test: "returns success, and a following GET shows status: 'frozen'."

Bob will often add a note on what it inferred rather than read in the request. Those become assumptions in requirements.md, and the interview in step 5 asks you to confirm them.

Read the pass conditions, not the tool table

The commands are reference. The pass conditions are what you're checking: could a test assert this? If a row says "works correctly," send it back.

Why ask what exists first. Requirements without testable criteria are wishes. Grounding them in the repo means:

  • pass conditions name real commands and fixtures, not a test strategy the agent invented
  • gaps in coverage surface now, not in Module 2

Why "one per outcome, each with a pass condition." Without it the agent tends to produce one criterion per test case instead of one per outcome. Tying the count to the request's outcomes keeps the list the same size as the request and traceable back to it.

Notice.

  • Anything in part 1 flagged as a gotcha. Those are the things that would have bitten you mid-implementation.
  • Any assumptions the agent declares. It's telling you what it decided for you.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 3. Surface open questions
items.text:
What open questions require my input that you can't settle from the code alone?

Expect. Two lists.

  • Needs your input: a handful of questions, each with the options and usually a lean. Every one should change the data model or what users see. If one doesn't, it belongs in the second list.
  • Defaults to veto: what the agent decided on its own by following the existing pattern, stated so you can overrule it. Bob will often include this. If it doesn't, the same list shows up in requirements.md in step 4.

Why ask at all. Some things the agent can't deduce from the code, and shouldn't. The ambiguous decisions are yours to make. This is a human ownership point: the feature's design choices stay with you.

Why a separate prompt. The real questions come from combining the three summaries: a fact from one set against a fact from another. Only the main conversation holds all three summaries, so only it can ask this. Folded into the fan-out, it would land at the bottom of a long response.

Why "that you can't settle from the code alone." AGENTS.md tells Bob to ask only when a decision changes scope, user-visible behavior or the data model, and default the rest. This phrasing invokes that rule, so you get the few decisions that are yours instead of a long list the memo code already answers.

Notice.

  • The second list exists at all. The agent is separating decisions that are yours from decisions it can make by precedent, which is the distinction the interview runs on.
  • The lean on each question. Take its word on the order. The answers are yours.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Part B: Decide and write (Plan mode)
items.text: Switch the mode selector to Plan. Plan mode can write files but still cannot run commands.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 4. Write requirements.md
items.text:
Write a `requirements.md` from this conversation, using the task and the validation criteria we just defined, the relevant files, and the open questions we had defined. Output a requirements artifact only. No plan or code yet.

Expect. A short chat summary and a new file. Open the file. Whatever its exact sections, it should carry everything the conversation produced:

  • the task and scope
  • the validation criteria, numbered
  • the open questions, each with options, a lean, and no decision yet
  • the relevant files and how the change will be verified

Bob may also tell you which parts of the file it verified itself and which it's carrying over from the subagents. That caveat is in the file too.

Read the open questions, skip the rest for now

The next step walks you through them. The criteria and file lists are for the agents that come after you.

Why this step exists. Everything the agent learned is in a conversation that will end. The prompt names the checklist of what has to survive: the task, the criteria, the files, the open questions. The file is the handoff artifact. The next agent reads it and knows everything except your decisions.

Notice. The open questions are still open. That's by design: the agent was asked for requirements, not a plan, and the decisions are yours. Human ownership means they stay open until you answer them.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 5. Settle the open questions
items.text:
Interview me about the open questions in @requirements.md.

Expect. Bob asks to activate the interview skill. Approve. Then:

  1. One question at a time, with its options and the proposed default, often as clickable buttons.
  2. After each answer, a line appended to a ## Decisions section in the file, recording what was decided and whether you accepted the default or overrode it.
  3. If the file has an assumptions section, each assumption read back for you to confirm or change.
  4. The open questions replaced with "None", the file marked decided, and a summary of the decisions in the chat.

Bob may point out places in the file that still refer to the old question numbers and offer to update them. Say yes.

The interview isn't finished until Bob says the file is marked decided. If it ends on a question ("do you confirm these?"), answer it. Otherwise the next step builds on an undecided file, and Bob will tell you so.

Why an interview. An interactive session is the easiest way to give feedback and stay in the loop. You iterate with the agent side by side instead of handing the design decisions to it. Human ownership again: you answer, the agent records.

Why a skill. Skills are reusable instruction sets that teach Bob new workflows: recipes it follows to do a kind of work the same way every time. The interview is one: a loop with a stopping rule and a side effect on a file:

  • ask → record → next, until no questions remain
  • then confirm assumptions, then mark the file decided, then stop

Typing that into a prompt every time is tedious and people skip steps. .bob/skills/interview/SKILL.md holds it.

Why one question at a time. Four answers in one paragraph is a block of text the agent has to parse and might misattribute. One answer per question lands in the file as one clean line with provenance: which question, what was decided, default accepted or overridden.

Notice.

  • This is the only step in the module where you supply something the agent couldn't get from the code.
  • The Decisions lines say default accepted or you overrode. That's the record of where your judgment went in.

Overrule at least one default

Accepting every default is handing the agent your design. Pick one and change it, if only to watch the file record it.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 6. Draft spec.md
items.text:
Using @requirements.md, draft a `spec.md`. Include the phases in dependency order, each naming the criteria it satisfies and how to check them. Every validation criterion must trace to a phase. No vague steps like "implement X", say what changes and where. Group changes into phases that can each be checked on their own; no phase without changes.

Expect. A chat summary and a new file. The summary usually has a table of phases with what each changes and which criteria it covers. The file has, for each phase:

  • Changes: files and functions, named
  • Satisfies: the criteria it covers
  • How to check: the commands to run and what passing looks like

and a traceability table at the end mapping every criterion to a phase. Bob will often add decisions it had to make that the requirements didn't cover, and sometimes a risk it wants you to rule on.

Read the decisions and risks first

Anything Bob flags there is a gap in requirements.md. Fixing it now costs one line in the file. Fixing it after Module 2 costs a rebuild.

Why each clause. These are what make it a spec in the SDD sense rather than a to-do list.

Clause What it does phases in dependency order contract before schema, service before routes, API before UI: each phase can be checked only once the one before it exists naming the criteria it satisfies and how to check them becomes the exit condition for each phase in Module 2 every validation criterion must trace to a phase produces the traceability table. Nothing from requirements gets dropped no vague steps like "implement X" a file, a function and a check instead of "add the endpoint" phases that can each be checked on their own, no phase without changes sets the phase size: big enough to be worth a check, never an empty setup phase

Notice.

  • The how-to-check sections are where the detail went. The criteria table was short. The checks cover the edge cases. That's the right place for them.
  • Decisions Bob made on its own. Each is a question the interview didn't ask. If one matters, say so now and have Bob update requirements.md before moving on.

Stop at a minimum viable spec

You're done when you understand every phase and would accept it as a plan from a colleague. Don't polish. Only requirements.md and spec.md carry forward. The conversation that produced them does not.

Secrets

Don't paste secrets into prompts, and don't have the agent open .env files. The repo's .env.example is the only env file it should see.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: What this module demonstrated
items.text:
• Short prompts in sequence, each one a question a developer would ask anyway. The structure that makes them work lives in AGENTS.md and the skill, not in the prompt text.
  • Subagents as context isolation: files read in disposable contexts, summaries in the one that persists.
  • Criteria grounded in tests that exist, not invented.
  • Human ownership of every design decision: the open questions are yours, the interview records your answers, and the spec is built from them. Module 2 builds from it.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Module 2: Spec Implementation
items.text:
One prompt, a new session, and a few minutes of watching. The spec from Module 1 does the work; you supervise against it.

Your design decisions are already in the spec. Human ownership here means holding the agent to it, not re-deciding.

Everything in a grey code block is pasted to Bob verbatim. The Expect and Notice notes describe what a good run looks like.

Before you start

  • requirements.md is marked decided and spec.md has its phases and traceability table. Nothing else from Module 1 carries forward.
  • git status shows only those two files as new. Everything else is clean. That clean tree is your undo button for this module.
  • The app is not running (Ctrl+C on npm run dev if it is). The tests don't need it, and a dev server holding the database open can confuse a migration.

items.title: 1. Start a fresh session
items.text:
Click New task in the Bob panel. Do not continue the Module 1 conversation.

Why. Module 1's conversation holds everything the agent picked up along the way: subagent summaries, dead ends, earlier drafts, your interview answers.

  • Run Module 2 in that session and you can't tell whether it built from the spec or from memory.
  • Run it fresh and spec.md has to carry the work on its own. The spec is the handoff; a cold context is what forces it to be one. If the build goes wrong, the spec was missing something, and that's a spec fix.
  • This is also the real case: the person implementing is often not the person who wrote the spec, and that session is gone.

items.title: 2. Set the guardrails
items.text:
Set the mode selector to Agent. In the Permissions dropdown, turn on the master Auto-approve switch. Bob will not ask you anything until it's done or stuck.

Why everything. Each phase is several file edits and at least one test run. Approving by hand turns a short build into a long clicking exercise, and you stop reading the cards after the fifth. This is the highest-autonomy stretch of the workshop, and you've earned it: every decision that reached this point went through you.

What's actually protecting you. Not the permissions. Three things:

  1. AGENTS.md says do not commit or push unless asked, so nothing leaves your working tree.
  2. The tree was clean, so git restore . undoes everything.
  3. The spec's per-phase checks give you a place to stop after every phase.

Permissions decide how often Bob asks. Those three decide how much damage a bad run can do.

items.title: 3. Hand it the spec
items.text:
Implement @spec.md phase by phase. Run each phase's checks and report before moving to the next.

Autonomy is highest here and human ownership lowest. What's left is implementation detail, and that's the agent's to hammer out on its own.

Expect. Bob reads spec.md, AGENTS.md, and the files the first phase names. Then, for each phase:

  • the edits the phase lists
  • that phase's checks, run
  • a short report: what changed, which check ran, pass or fail

At the end, a summary of what every phase changed. A few things look like trouble and aren't: a check that fails once and gets fixed and rerun (that's the loop working), and a long pause on the first phase while it reads.

Why the prompt is short. Everything that would normally go in a long implementation prompt is already in the files Bob reads. The spec says what to build and how to check it. AGENTS.md says how code is written here, which commands to run, and what not to do. The prompt only has to say follow the spec and stop and check at each phase boundary. If you find yourself adding instructions to this prompt, they belong in one of those two files instead.

Why "report before moving to the next." Without it Bob still runs the checks but tends to batch the reporting at the end. With it, every phase boundary becomes a point where you can read a short report and decide to let it continue. You are not approving each phase (Auto-approve is on), but you can interrupt at any boundary.

items.title: The loop
items.text:
What you're watching is a loop, and naming its parts is what lets you reason about it when it misbehaves:

Part In this run Goal The current phase's Changes and Satisfies lines in spec.md Act Edit the named files, write the named tests Observe Run that phase's how-to-check commands Decide Green → next phase. Red → read the output, fix, run again Carry forward Only what the next phase needs: the spec, the files on disk, the test results

The spec is the loop condition. A phase is done when its checks pass, and the agent can't declare itself done any other way. Compare that with an agent given "implement the freeze feature" and no spec: the loop has no exit condition except the agent's own opinion that it's finished.

Notice.

  • The reports stay short. Bob reads a great deal while building, but the summary at each boundary is a few lines. That's the same context discipline as Module 1's subagents, applied inside one session.
  • Where it runs tests. If it runs npm test -w api after a web change, or runs the whole suite after every edit, the spec's how-to-check section was too loose. Note it; that's a Module 1 fix for next time.
  • The context counter. It climbs through the run. If a phase fails repeatedly, the counter is the first thing to check: an agent with several failed attempts in its context tends to repeat them.

items.title: 4. Supervise against the spec
items.text:
You're not reviewing code yet. You're checking that each phase report matches what the spec said that phase would do. Keep spec.md open beside the chat.

Three things to compare at each boundary:

  1. Files. The report names the files it changed. The spec's Changes list names the files it should have. Same list?
  2. Check. The report names the command it ran. The spec's how-to-check section names the command. Same command, and did it actually pass, or did Bob say "tests pass" without output?
  3. Scope. Anything in the report the spec didn't ask for? A refactor, an extra endpoint, a helpful improvement. Those are the things that break later.

items.title: If a phase drifts
items.text:
Phase N was supposed to X. It did Y. Fix it to match the spec — don't change the spec.

Expect. Bob rereads the phase, undoes or adjusts the extra work, reruns the check, and reports again.

Why "don't change the spec." An agent that notices a mismatch between its work and the spec will sometimes resolve it by editing the spec. That erases the evidence and makes the next phase build on the drift. The spec is the contract; if it's wrong, you change it deliberately in Module 1's terms, not as a side effect of a fix.

items.title: If a phase fails and keeps failing
items.text:
Let it try twice. On the third red run, stop it and read the failure output yourself. Usually it's one of:

  • the spec's check references a test the changes never created (spec fix)
  • a command can't run because something is still holding a resource, usually the dev server (stop it, rerun)
  • a type error in a file the spec didn't name (one-line hint to Bob)

items.title: If it derails
items.text:
git restore .
git clean -n

Rollback (the icon on your message in the chat) undoes what Bob did in this task. git restore . undoes everything in tracked files regardless of which task did it. Run git clean -n to list new untracked files; delete by hand only the ones Bob created. Then start a new task and paste the prompt again.

Never git clean -f or git clean -fd

It deletes every untracked file, including requirements.md, spec.md, api/.env and the database. There is no undo. git clean -n with the n lists without deleting; that's the only form to use here.

items.title: 5. Confirm the finish
items.text:
When Bob reports the last phase green, run the checks yourself in the terminal:

npm run typecheck -w api && npm run typecheck -w web
npm test -w api && npm test -w web
git status

Green, green, and a git status that shows changes only under api/ and web/ plus the migration folder.

Start the app (npm run dev), log in as a supervisor, open an account, and freeze it. The status badge changes, the reason shows, the audit log has an entry. Unfreeze it. Thirty seconds.

Leave everything uncommitted. Module 3 reviews the working tree against main.

items.title: What this module demonstrated
items.text:
• A fresh session proves the spec carries the implementation. Nothing learned in Module 1's conversation was needed.
  • The implementation prompt is short because the spec and AGENTS.md are not. Instructions you'd put in the prompt belong in those files.
  • Autonomy is set by three things: what the agent is forbidden to do (AGENTS.md), what can be undone (clean tree, git restore .), and where it must stop and report (phase boundaries). Permissions only set how often it asks. You earned that autonomy in Module 1; here you enforce it.
  • A loop needs an exit condition the agent doesn't control. Here that's the spec's checks.
  • Supervising means comparing reports to the spec, not reading code. The code review is Module 3.

items.title: Module 3: Validation
items.text:
Module 2 ended with every phase check green. Green means the agent built what the spec said. It doesn't mean the spec said the right thing, and it doesn't mean the code is right in ways the spec never mentioned. Validation asks the two questions green checks can't:

  1. Does the code match the spec? (implementation drift)
  2. Does the spec match the need? (spec drift)

In spec-driven development, validation validates the spec as much as the code, and the loop closes by changing the spec, not by patching around it.

Mechanism Reads Catches /review the diff code that's wrong on its own terms: bugs, conventions, weak tests Independent reviewer (Ask mode) the diff, spec.md, requirements.md code that doesn't match the spec; risks the spec didn't cover Human gate both reports, plus what you know about the product whether the spec itself needs to change, and what the team will accept

Human ownership comes back up here. The agents find; you decide.

Everything in a grey code block is pasted to Bob or the terminal verbatim. The Expect and Notice notes describe what a good run looks like.

Before you start

  • Module 2's build is finished and uncommitted. git status shows changes under api/ and web/, plus requirements.md and spec.md as new files.
  • The dev server is stopped.

items.title: 1. Look at the blast radius
items.text:
In the terminal:

git diff --stat main

Then open one changed file you understand and read one new function. Not the whole diff. One function, and ask yourself whether you'd have written it that way.

Why first. Before any agent tells you what to think about the code, get your own impression of its size and shape:

  • A diff much bigger than you expected is a finding by itself.
  • Reading one function keeps you reading code in this module, not just reports.

Notice. Files you didn't expect. If the diff touches something the spec never named, write it down; it goes to the gate.

items.title: 2. Built-in review: is the code right on its own terms?
items.text:
In the Bob panel, type /review. Set the comparison branch to main, tick Include uncommitted changes, and start it. It runs auto-approved and takes a minute or two.

Expect. Findings in the Bob Findings tab, grouped by file: the kind of thing a careful colleague flags on a pull request. Some will be sharp, some pedantic, and one or two will be wrong.

Read them. Click Go to file on the two or three that look real. Do not click Fix with Bob, on any of them, yet.

Why not Fix with Bob. The button collapses two steps that have to stay separate:

  1. Is this finding right?
  2. Do we want this change?

This reviewer reads the diff and nothing else. It doesn't know that a duplicated check might be deliberate, or that an error message's wording came from an interview decision. Fixing before deciding puts the reviewer's opinion into your code with no record of why. You decide in step 4.

What this reviewer can and can't tell you. It's good at the first question in the table and badly placed for the second. It has never seen the spec, so it can tell you whether the code is tidy, not whether the code does what was agreed. That's what the next reviewer is for.

items.title: 3. Independent review: does the code match the spec?
items.text:
Start a new task. Set the mode to Ask. Paste:

Review the diff against @spec.md and @requirements.md: does the code match the spec, is it safe for a regulated fintech app, and would the tests fail if a requirement were broken? Skip what matches. Report what matters and mark which findings need a human decision.

Expect. Bob runs git diff itself, reads the two markdown files, then the changed files. A few minutes. Length varies: sometimes a short report, sometimes a longer one where Bob clears items as it goes and ends with a summary. Either way, look for two groups:

  • Needs a human decision: the code did what the spec said and the spec didn't say enough. A failure mode the request never mentioned, a message that's correct but confusing, a field stored but never shown. Those aren't code corrections; the spec was silent on something the need required. That's spec drift.
  • Tests that wouldn't catch a break: assertions that would still pass if the behavior were removed. These need no decision, just a test.

Bob may also say what it couldn't verify from Ask mode, usually that it didn't run the test commands. You did, at the end of Module 2.

If the report is long, read the end first

The findings are at the bottom. Anything above them that ends in "no issue" is Bob's working.

Why a new task. This reviewer must not have built the code. The Module 2 session knows every decision it made and will defend them; it reads its own code the way you read your own prose, seeing what it meant rather than what's there.

Why Ask mode. Ask mode cannot edit files. A reviewer that can fix things will fix things, and you're back to the Fix with Bob problem with less visibility. Making the fix impossible, rather than asking it to refrain, is the mechanism.

Why each clause.

Clause What it does does the code match the spec, is it safe, would the tests fail the three ways a feature fails review in a regulated codebase: doesn't match what was agreed, unsafe, untested in a way that lets it rot. The safety question is what lets the reviewer see past the spec. skip what matches without it the report opens with paragraphs confirming what's fine and runs out of room for what isn't report what matters the confirmed findings with file and line, so you can check one by opening one file mark which findings need a human decision separates findings with one right answer (a missing test) from tradeoffs. The gate goes through the second group only.

Notice.

  • Findings /review raised that this reviewer didn't, and the reverse. Neither is the better reviewer; they hold different context, so they see different things. Module 1 was about keeping context out of a conversation; this is about choosing what to put in.
  • Anything flagged that the spec didn't ask for. A reviewer that only walks the spec's list misses scope creep.
  • The human-decision group. Each item there is a candidate change to the spec, not to the code.

items.title: 4. The human gate: does the spec match the need?
items.text:
Before anything gets fixed, answer these three questions.

  1. Does the code do what we agreed? Every requirement has a phase, every phase passed its check, nothing in the diff is outside the spec. If not: which gap, and is it the code that's wrong or the spec?
  2. For each item marked as needing a decision: fix now, follow-up, or reject? One sentence why. Say for each fix now whether it's a code correction (the spec was right, the agent drifted) or a spec change (the spec was wrong or silent).
  3. Would the tests catch it breaking? If someone removed the role check tomorrow, which test goes red? If the answer is none, that's a fix before merge whatever the reviewers said.

Keep your answers to one line each. They're the input to the next step.

Why the gate is human. Both reviewers produce findings. Neither can decide what the team is willing to ship, whether a tradeoff goes the team's way, or whether a follow-up is really going to happen. That judgment doesn't delegate. This is the human ownership point of the module.

items.title: 5. Close the loop through the spec
items.text:
Don't fix the code directly. Start a new task in Agent mode with Auto-approve on, and give it the gate's answers:

Update @spec.md with these review decisions: [your one-line answers from the gate]. Amend only the affected phase and add a Review section recording each decision. Then re-implement that phase and run its checks.

Expect. Bob edits the affected phase, adds the Review section, then makes the change, runs that phase's checks, and reports.

Why through the spec.

  • A fix made straight in the code leaves spec.md describing something that no longer exists. The next person, or the next agent, builds from the old version.
  • Routing it through the spec keeps the spec true and records why it changed. You made the decision; the agent is the clerk, as in the interview.
  • It's the same loop as Module 2, one more time: the spec changed, so a phase gets rebuilt and checked. A finding that overturns an interview decision goes further back, to requirements.md, and that's the expensive path by design.

Swap diffs

If there's time, run step 3's prompt against a neighbor's working tree instead of your own. You'll read their findings more skeptically than your own.

Don't commit from the lab machine

The working tree stays uncommitted. The lab machines are wiped; copy requirements.md and spec.md out if you want to keep them.

items.title: What this module demonstrated
items.text:
• Green checks prove the agent built the spec. Validation asks whether the code matches the spec and whether the spec matches the need; different questions, different readers.
  • Two reviewers with different context find different things. /review has only the diff; the independent reviewer has the spec too. Neither replaces the other.
  • A reviewer that cannot fix is a reviewer you can trust to only report. Ask mode enforces it.
  • The findings that matter most are the ones the spec was silent on. Those are spec problems: you decide at the gate, an agent records the decision in spec.md, an agent rebuilds the phase, and the checks run the same way as the original.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Complete these steps on your lab machine before the first module. Everything runs inside the Linux environment (WSL) on the machine. The app uses SQLite, an embedded database file, so there is no server or container to set up.

Own machine?

These instructions are for the provisioned lab machines. If you're on your own machine, ask a facilitator.

items.title: 1. Open the Linux terminal
items.text: Open Fedora Linux from the Start menu (or wsl.exe on the desktop). Every command below runs in this terminal, not in PowerShell or Command Prompt.

items.title: 2. Install make
items.text:
The SQLite driver compiles a small native component on first install, and the image ships without make:

sudo yum install -y make

items.title: 3. Confirm the toolchain
items.text:
node --version && npm --version && git --version

You should see Node v22.x or newer and version numbers for npm and git. If anything is missing, flag a facilitator before going further.

items.title: 4. Clone and set up
items.text:
Switch to your home directory:

cd ~

Then clone the repo and run setup:

git clone https://github.com/hbattu73/finch-financial.git
cd finch-financial
npm run setup

npm run setup installs dependencies, creates api/.env with working defaults, creates the SQLite database, and seeds it. It takes about a minute. Ignore the npm warn deprecated lines and the vulnerabilities summary at the end. Neither affects the workshop.

items.title: 5. Start the app
items.text:
npm run dev

This starts the API (port 3000) and the web app (port 5173) in one terminal. Open http://localhost:5173 in the Windows browser. WSL forwards the port automatically. Log in with any seeded user. All users share the password Password123!.

You should see a list of customer accounts with status badges, filters by status and name, and an account detail page with transactions, memos and an audit log. If you can browse accounts, the app is ready. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

items.title: 6. Connect Bob IDE to the Linux environment
items.text:
Bob IDE needs an extension to see the Linux filesystem.

  1. Open IBM Bob from the Start menu.
  2. Open the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for Open Remote - WSL (publisher: jeanp413), and install it.
  3. Press Ctrl+Shift+P, type WSL, and choose Connect to WSL. A new Bob window opens inside the Linux environment. Its title bar shows the distro name.
  4. In that window, File → Open Folder and open /home/<your-user>/finch-financial.
  5. If Bob asks whether you trust the authors of the folder, click Yes, I trust the authors.

You should see AGENTS.md, product-requests.md and PROMPTS.md in the file tree, and the Bob icon in the activity bar on the left. If the icon is missing or the panel is blank, see Troubleshooting below.

Open the Bob panel and check Settings → Skills: interview should be listed with scope Workspace. You're ready.

items.title: Next Steps
items.text: Proceed to the Presentation.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Both test suites are standalone: no running server and no database setup. Your development data is never touched.

npm test              # everything
npm test -w api       # one workspace
npm test -w web

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
npm run setup fails building better-sqlite3

The error block mentions node-gyp rebuild. make isn't installed. Run sudo yum install -y make, then npm run setup again.

localhost:5173 doesn't load in the Windows browser

Confirm npm run dev is still running in the Linux terminal. If it is and the page still won't load, run hostname -I in the terminal and use that address in place of localhost.

Port 3000 or 5173 is already in use

Another process is holding the port, usually a previous npm run dev. Find and stop it: 

lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill
lsof -ti:5173 | xargs kill

Bob can't see the repo files

Bob has to open the folder from inside the Linux environment. If you opened it via a Windows path (\\wsl$\... or C:\...), close that window and repeat step 6.

Bob icon missing or chat panel blank

First, look at the bottom-left of the status bar for Restricted Mode. If it's there, click it and choose Trust, then reload the window.

If that doesn't fix it, run the repair script:

  1. Close Bob IDE completely.
  2. Expand the block below, copy the whole script, and save it to your Windows Desktop as fix-bob-ide.ps1. In Notepad: paste, File → Save As, set Save as type to All Files, name it fix-bob-ide.ps1.
  3. Open PowerShell on the Windows side (not the Linux terminal) and run: 
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\fix-bob-ide.ps1"
  4. It prints what it changed. Relaunch Bob from the Start menu and repeat step 6 above.

Don't paste the script straight into the PowerShell window. It has to run from a file. Flag a facilitator if you'd rather have someone run it with you.

fix-bob-ide.ps1 (click to expand) 
# fix-bob-ide.ps1
# Fixes IBM Bob IDE showing a blank panel when launched from C:\Windows\System32.
#
# Root cause: the IDE inherits System32 as its working directory from the Start Menu
# shortcut (no working directory set). VS Code treats System32 as an untrusted
# workspace and disables the bob-code extension, leaving a blank panel.
#
# This script applies three independent fixes; each is idempotent and reports its own result:
#   1. Disables workspace trust in the IDE's user settings.json (no dependencies)
#   2. Adds C:\Windows\System32 to the trusted-folders database (requires Python)
#   3. Sets C:\Users\<username> as the Start Menu shortcut's working directory
#
# Run this script WHILE THE IBM BOB IDE IS CLOSED.

param(
    [switch]$SkipSettings,
    [switch]$SkipTrustDb,
    [switch]$SkipShortcut
)

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$results = @()

# --- Verify IBM Bob IDE is not running (match by path, not by guessed process name) ---
$running = Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.Path -and $_.Path -like "*IBM Bob*" }
if ($running) {
    Write-Error "IBM Bob IDE appears to be running ($($running[0].ProcessName)). Close it and run this script again."
    exit 1
}

$userDir = "$env:APPDATA\IBM Bob\User"
if (-not (Test-Path $userDir)) {
    Write-Error "Could not find IBM Bob user data at: $userDir. Has the IDE been launched at least once?"
    exit 1
}

# --- Fix 1: disable workspace trust in settings.json ---
if (-not $SkipSettings) {
    Write-Host "Fix 1: disabling workspace trust in settings.json..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
    try {
        $settingsPath = Join-Path $userDir "settings.json"
        $settings = @{}
        if (Test-Path $settingsPath) {
            $raw = Get-Content $settingsPath -Raw
            if ($raw.Trim()) {
                $obj = $raw | ConvertFrom-Json
                $obj.PSObject.Properties | ForEach-Object { $settings[$_.Name] = $_.Value }
            }
        }
        if ($settings["security.workspace.trust.enabled"] -eq $false) {
            $results += "Fix 1: already applied."
        } else {
            $settings["security.workspace.trust.enabled"] = $false
            $settings | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10 | Set-Content -Path $settingsPath -Encoding UTF8
            $results += "Fix 1: workspace trust disabled."
        }
    } catch {
        $results += "Fix 1: FAILED - $($_.Exception.Message)"
    }
}

# --- Fix 2: trust C:\Windows\System32 in the workspace trust database ---
if (-not $SkipTrustDb) {
    Write-Host "Fix 2: patching workspace trust database..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
    $db = Join-Path $userDir "globalStorage\state.vscdb"
    $py = Get-Command python -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    $pyOk = $false
    if ($py) {
        # Rule out the Microsoft Store stub, which exists but does nothing useful
        $ver = & python --version 2>&1
        if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0 -and "$ver" -match "^Python 3") { $pyOk = $true }
    }

    if (-not (Test-Path $db)) {
        $results += "Fix 2: SKIPPED - state.vscdb not found at $db."
    } elseif (-not $pyOk) {
        $results += "Fix 2: SKIPPED - Python 3 not available on Windows (Fix 1 covers the same symptom)."
    } else {
        $pyScript = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName() + ".py"
        $pyLines = @(
            "import sqlite3, json, sys",
            "db  = sys.argv[1]",
            "key = 'content.trust.model.key'",
            "conn = sqlite3.connect(db)",
            "cur  = conn.cursor()",
            "cur.execute('SELECT value FROM ItemTable WHERE key=?', (key,))",
            "row = cur.fetchone()",
            "data = json.loads(row[0]) if row else {'uriTrustInfo': []}",
            "entries = data.get('uriTrustInfo', [])",
            "already = any(e.get('uri', {}).get('path', '').lower() == '/c:/windows/system32' for e in entries)",
            "if already:",
            "    print('already trusted')",
            "else:",
            "    entries.append({'uri': {'`$mid': 1, 'path': '/c:/Windows/System32', 'scheme': 'file'}, 'trusted': True})",
            "    data['uriTrustInfo'] = entries",
            "    val = json.dumps(data)",
            "    if row:",
            "        cur.execute('UPDATE ItemTable SET value=? WHERE key=?', (val, key))",
            "    else:",
            "        cur.execute('INSERT INTO ItemTable (key, value) VALUES (?, ?)', (key, val))",
            "    conn.commit()",
            "    print('trusted')",
            "conn.close()"
        )
        Set-Content -Path $pyScript -Encoding UTF8 -Value ($pyLines -join "`n")
        $out = & python $pyScript $db 2>&1
        $code = $LASTEXITCODE
        Remove-Item $pyScript -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        if ($code -eq 0) {
            $results += "Fix 2: $out."
        } else {
            $results += "Fix 2: FAILED - $out"
        }
    }
}

# --- Fix 3: set working directory on the Start Menu / Desktop shortcut ---
if (-not $SkipShortcut) {
    Write-Host "Fix 3: fixing shortcut working directory..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
    $shortcutPaths = @(
        "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\IBM Bob.lnk",
        "$env:PROGRAMDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\IBM Bob.lnk",
        "$env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\IBM Bob.lnk"
    )
    $found = $false
    foreach ($path in $shortcutPaths) {
        if (-not (Test-Path $path)) { continue }
        $found = $true
        try {
            $shell    = New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell
            $shortcut = $shell.CreateShortcut($path)
            if ($shortcut.WorkingDirectory -eq $env:USERPROFILE) {
                $results += "Fix 3: $path already correct."
            } else {
                $shortcut.WorkingDirectory = $env:USERPROFILE
                $shortcut.Save()
                $results += "Fix 3: $path updated."
            }
        } catch {
            $results += "Fix 3: could not update $path - $($_.Exception.Message) (likely needs admin; Fix 1 still applies)."
        }
    }
    if (-not $found) {
        $results += "Fix 3: no shortcut found at the standard locations."
    }
}

Write-Host ""
Write-Host "Results:" -ForegroundColor Green
$results | ForEach-Object { Write-Host "  $_" }
Write-Host ""
Write-Host "Launch IBM Bob from the Start Menu. If the panel is still blank, check the status bar for 'Restricted Mode' and click Trust." -ForegroundColor Green
git status shows package-lock.json modified right after setup

npm on this image rewrites some lockfile metadata. It's harmless. If you want a clean tree, run git restore package-lock.json.

Reset data at any time

The seed script is idempotent. To restore the original workshop data: 

npm run seed
To start completely fresh: 
rm api/finch.db
npm run setup
